rows: A honeybee worker resolves gratings of about a quarter of a cycle per degree, roughly one two-hundredth of a person's sharpness. Bumblebees and stingless bees fall in the same range.

Bees have three colour receptors, peaking in the ultraviolet near 340 to 350 nanometres, in the blue near 430 to 445 nanometres and in the green near 530 to 556 nanometres. The view shows the ultraviolet as blue, the blue as green and the green as red, so the picture is not a true colour match.
A bee sees almost all around itself, about 300 degrees across the horizontal. The picture is squeezed toward this wide field.
Bees hold their gaze still between quick head turns that last about 45 to 135 milliseconds. The view jumps in short steps to show this.
The sharpness, the glow of movement, the slow pace, the gaze timing and the palette of this view are the app's own choices. The records give the bee's limits, but not how they look on a screen.

claims.how: The honeybee worker's highest resolved grating is 0.26 cycles per degree, as the record states.
The bee field of view is given as about 300 degrees horizontally, graded g because the record is a general figure for bees cited from an older study.

quotes.quote: They found that the highest spatial frequency reliably resolved by the bees was 0.26 cycle deg−1, with no evidence of a difference in acuity between horizontal and vertical gratings.
Bees can see ~300° horizontally on the body plane with low spatial resolution for peripheral ommatidia

spec.cue: Hold still, and the spider's eyes will find you. Its front pair is sharp and narrow, and its side eyes watch the rest of the room for movement.

cpd.note: Portia fimbriata principal eye; the picture uses the best measured acuity in the family

fov.note: whole-animal field from the secondary eyes near 300 to 360 degrees; the picture uses the lower end

fovea.note: scale of the sharp middle; the principal-eye strip is about 2 degrees wide against a person's central field, and the app chose the scale from that

gate.note: how far still things fade; the side eyes respond only to movement, and the app chose the strength

persist.note: how long the picture lingers, chosen by the app

rate.note: no record gives a playback rate; flicker fusion is up to 40 Hz, well above a phone

fall.note: how fast sharpness falls with light, chosen by the app; the principal eyes need bright light

sat.note: colour saturation, chosen by the app

uvBlue.note: how much blue reads as ultraviolet, chosen by the app; the phone has no ultraviolet channel

gain.note: brightness gain, chosen by the app

rows: Two colours in the front eyes
The principal eyes of Saitis barbipes carry an ultraviolet pigment and a green pigment, peaking near 359 nm and 526 nm. No red receptor was found, so red and black look much alike to this view.

The front eyes of Portia fimbriata resolve about 12.4 cycles per degree, close to a bird of prey. Most salticids are far less sharp, so this picture is drawn at the sharpness of the best measured case.
Each principal retina is a thin upright strip, about 2 degrees wide and 21 degrees high in Phidippus johnsoni. Only that strip is sharp at once, and the eye moves it back and forth across the scene.
The side eyes of salticids together see almost all the way round, about 300 to 360 degrees, and they respond to movement. A person sees about 180 degrees.

The side eyes of Menemerus semilimbatus respond to moving targets and show a clear peak in turning near 50 degrees from straight ahead. Stationary targets never start a turn, which is why still things fade in this picture.
The brightness, the lingering of the picture and the way sharpness falls with dim light are the app's own choices, set from the records but not measured in one animal.

claims.how: Portia fimbriata principal eye acuity is stated as 12.4 cycles per degree in R1.
The secondary eyes give a field near 300 degrees (R35) and the whole animal near 360 degrees (R23); 300 is the lower end of the cited range, and the grade is g because these are family-level figures.
The matrix uses the UV peak at 359 nm and the green peak at 526 nm measured in Saitis barbipes.
The principal retina is about 2 degrees wide (R14); the scale 2.2 is the app's choice set against a person's central field, so it is invented and graded g only for its basis.
R369 says the side eyes are blind to stationary objects; the strength 0.6 is the app's choice from that statement, so it is invented and graded g.

the remaining six, smaller eyes providing a near 300° field of view
Combined, the four pairs of eyes give the spider a 360° field of view.
we find clear evidence for photoreceptor classes with maximal sensitivity in the UV (359 nm) and green (526 nm)
clear evidence for photoreceptor classes with maximal sensitivity in the UV (359 nm) and green (526 nm)
inconclusive evidence for a photoreceptor maximally sensitive in the blue (451 nm), and no evidence for a red photoreceptor.
the jumping spider *Portia* fi*mbriata* has acuity on par with passerine birds, at 13 cpd
the angular subtense of the retinae in object space (about 21 ° x 2° for layers 1 and 2) is the same in both species
the angular subtense of the retinae in object space (about 21 ° x 2° for layers 1 and 2) is the same in both species
It consists of an oscillatory, side-to-side movement of the retinae across the stimulus, with a period of 1-2 sec.
grant the spider an almost 360° field of view
there was a clear peak in responses at around ±50 deg for the ALE treatment (Fig. 3).
the system behaves as though it were completely blind to stationary objects.
Stationary targets never initiate saccades, although small movements of targets already within the retinal fields of view are effective stimuli.

rows: A scorpion's median and lateral eyes together give a view of all round its body, which is why the picture reaches all the way round. The figure is reported from earlier work and not measured in these species.
Scorpion eyes peak in the blue-green, with a green peak at 525 nm in one set of species and a blue peak at 470 nm in another, so the picture leans blue-green.
The lateral eyes have a secondary ultraviolet sensitivity, and scorpions are attracted to 399 nm light at night, so the picture gives ultraviolet a small share.
Scorpions have eyes that detect very low light, and lateral eyes in one buthid are about ten log units more sensitive than the median eyes, so the dark picture is brighter than the day picture.
Scorpions read the world mostly through their legs, pedipalps and pectines, which the camera does not record.
How sharp the picture is, how fast it blurs in dim light, how much still things fade, and the palette's greying are the app's guesses, since no record gives them.

rows: Octopus measured at 3.1 to 6.8 cycles per degree in behavioural tests, with one octopus at 12.2. Squid near 0.6 to 6.6. The picture is blurred to a middle value of 6 cycles per degree.
Most cephalopods have one visual pigment, and the octopus and squid studied did not tell colours apart. The picture is drawn in brightness alone, with almost no colour.
A squid of 7 days sees about 311 degrees around itself and an adult of 27 days about 323, while an octopus has no significant binocular overlap. The picture is squeezed toward 300 degrees.
The octopus pupil is round in darkness and narrows to a horizontal slit in bright light. The picture uses a slit that is horizontal.
The pupil closes to about 10 per cent of its dark-adapted area in bright light and takes about one second to do so. The picture closes the pupil in bright places and opens it in the dark.
Octopus and squid sense the plane of polarised light, so the picture shows a faint shimmer that follows that plane.
The mapping to one colour channel, the sharpness fall, the streak in the middle, the gain and the glow are the app's own settings, set inside the measured range.

rows: The sharp eyes at the front hold two kinds of colour receptor, one most sensitive to ultraviolet near 360 nanometres and one to green near 530. With two kinds, the picture has two colour channels and no red.
The two front eyes see sharply in a very small field of about 5 degrees. A typical species resolves about 3.8 cycles per degree there, around an eighth of your sharpness.
Six smaller eyes sit around the head and cover almost the whole circle. They give one channel of vision at about 1.3 cycles per degree, so the edges of the picture are soft and grey.
The side eyes behave as if completely blind to stationary things, and a target in view turns the spider only when it moves. Outside the sharp patch, only movement draws attention.
The spider sweeps its sharp patch side to side across what it inspects, about every 1.2 seconds, and twists it 20 to 30 degrees, holding each extreme for several seconds.

The colour mapping from two pigments, the grey outside the patch, the full fade of still things there, the size of the patch, the sharpness numbers carried over to the whole picture and the way the scan is drawn are choices of the app.

rows: An octopus resolves about 12 cycles per degree and a squid about 6.6, against your 30. A cuttlefish is put near 8. Newly hatched squid see far coarser, near 0.6. The picture is blurred to 8, a middle value that no single species is said to match.

Almost every octopus, squid and cuttlefish has one visual pigment, with its peak between 470 and 500 nanometres. An Octopus tetricus is described as colour-blind, and a cuttlefish retina cannot respond to colour. Cuttlefish cannot see red light. The picture loses its colour and keeps a brightness that favours blue-green.

Young oval squid take in about 312 degrees around them. One cuttlefish eye covers about 253 degrees, and the two eyes overlap by 86 degrees in front. Octopuses have no significant overlap. The camera holds a slice of this field and the rest is invented.
An octopus pupil is round in the dark and closes to a horizontal slit in bright light. Cuttlefish and Eledone can shrink theirs to 3% of the full area. The picture uses the horizontal slit.

Octopus photoreceptors crowd into a central horizontal stripe, about 55,000 per square millimetre against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edge. Squid and cuttlefish have a similar streak. The picture is sharper along a horizontal band, and how much sharper is the app's choice.

A squid loses flicker near 51 flashes a second, a cuttlefish near 30, and an octopus between 20 and 72 depending on the light. You lose it near 60. Squid time runs a little slower than yours and cuttlefish time at about half.

Octopuses respond to polarized light at a very fine threshold, a median of 0.010 on the polarization distance scale. The cephalopod retina has two sensitive planes, one horizontal and one vertical. The picture can show an overlay of where polarized light would stand out, and its look is the app's.

The single value of 8 cycles per degree, the 312 degree field taken from young squid, the strength of the sharp streak, the pace of 0.85, the horizontal pupil, the one-pigment colour matrix and the polarization overlay are the app's own settings, set inside the measured range.

claims.how: The value 8 equals the cuttlefish figure in R14 and lies between the squid figure in R6 and the octopus figure in R7.
The value 312 degrees is the visual field of 14 day old oval squid in R25.
A single pigment peaking at 485 nm, the peak given for Hapalochlaena maculosa in R46 and Octopus australis in R47, is turned into a one-channel colour matrix.
The matrix is built from one pigment peak at 485 nm, which equals the peak in R46 and R47, and the weighting into a colour matrix is the app's own.
50.8 Hz from R82 divided by an assumed person's pace of 60 Hz is about 0.85.
30 Hz from R84 divided by an assumed person's pace of 60 Hz is 0.5.
